title: Linux Security Features: Namespaces & Capabilities 🧱
description: Discover how Docker uses Linux kernel features to isolate containers and limit their power.

slides.title: Containers Are Not Magic 🔮
slides.content:
# The Kernel Does the Heavy Lifting

A container is just a group of processes with restricted views of the system. Docker achieves this using two main Linux kernel features:

- **Namespaces**: limit what a process can **see** (processes, network, filesystem, etc.).
- **Control Groups (cgroups)**: limit what a process can **use** (CPU, memory, disk I/O).

We’ll focus on namespaces and another key feature: **capabilities**.

slides.title: Linux Namespaces – The Walls 🧱
slides.content:
# Isolated Views

Each container gets its own set of namespaces:
- **PID namespace** – the container sees only its own processes (PID 1 inside = main process).
- **Network namespace** – its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing tables.
- **Mount namespace** – its own filesystem root (the image).
- **UTS namespace** – its own hostname and domain name.
- **IPC namespace** – isolated inter‑process communication.
- **User namespace** (optional) – maps UIDs inside the container to different UIDs on the host.

These namespaces create the illusion of a separate machine.

quizData.question: What does the PID namespace give a container?

options.text: Its own process tree, with PID 1 being the main container process

quizData.explanation: PID namespace isolates processes. Inside the container, only its own processes are visible, and the main process appears as PID 1.

slides.title: Capabilities – Fine‑Grained Root 🎛️
slides.content:
# Not All Root Is Equal

Traditionally, the `root` user can do anything. Linux **capabilities** break this power into small pieces (e.g., `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `CAP_SYS_TIME`).

Docker starts containers with a limited set of capabilities (even when running as root inside the container). You can further drop or add capabilities.

**Default list** includes `CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `FSETID`, `FOWNER`, `SETGID`, `SETUID`, `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, etc.

> Important: The container’s root user is **not the same as the host’s root**. It is confined by capabilities and namespaces.

slides.title: Check Container Capabilities 🔍
slides.content: See the capabilities of a running container:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Run a container and inspect its capabilities
docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'apk add libcap; capsh --print'

# Drop all capabilities and add only what you need
docker run --rm --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE alpine sh

quizData.question: What does `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` do?

options.text: Grants the container full root privileges
Removes all capabilities except the ability to bind to low ports

quizData.explanation: It starts with an empty set of capabilities and adds only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, severely limiting what the container can do.

slides.title: Seccomp & AppArmor/SELinux 🔒
slides.content:
# Additional Layers

- **Seccomp** (Secure Computing Mode): filters the system calls a container can make. Docker uses a default seccomp profile that blocks around 44 of 300+ syscalls (e.g., `reboot`, `mount`).
- **AppArmor / SELinux**: mandatory access control systems that can apply policies to containers.

You can apply custom profiles with `--security-opt seccomp=profile.json` or `--security-opt apparmor=myprofile`.

> These are advanced but powerful tools for defence in depth.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Least Privilege
Always drop capabilities you don’t need. Even the default set may be too generous for a simple stateless app.
